title: Storage Systems
summary: Block, file, or object? B-tree or LSM? Every byte your system keeps lives on one of these abstractions, and the wrong pick quietly caps your scale, cost, and durability for years.

blocks.markdown:
Storage comes in three shapes and two engine families — that's the whole map.

- **Block** — raw addressable blocks, one host owns it. The database's playground.
- **File** — a tree of directories with `open`/`read`/`write` and POSIX semantics.
- **Object** — a flat bucket of immutable blobs reached by an HTTP API (S3). The cloud workhorse.
- **Engines** split into **B-trees** (update in place, fast reads) and **LSM-trees** (append now, merge later, fast writes).

blocks.subTitle: What to reach for
blocks.markdown:
Match the abstraction to what you actually need.

| Need | Reach for |
|---|---|
| A disk a database manages itself | Block (EBS, SAN) |
| Shared files with directories | File (NFS, EFS) |
| Cheap, massive, durable blobs | Object (S3, GCS) |
| Write-heavy logs / time-series / KV | LSM engine |
| Read-heavy transactional workload | B-tree engine |
| Scan few columns over many rows | Columnar store |

blocks.subTitle: Block, file, object as layers
blocks.markdown:
Think of the three shapes as layers, each built on the one below.

![Object storage layout: bucket, key, index, replicas](assets/storage-systems/object-storage-layout.svg)

- **Block** = numbered sectors on a raw disk, attached to one host. Lowest latency, capped at one volume.
- **File** = a file system over blocks, inventing folders, names, and byte-range edits. Limited by metadata scale.
- **Object** = a separate distributed service: PUT/GET by key, no POSIX, near-infinite scale with built-in redundancy.
- Change granularity drops as you climb: any block → any byte range → whole-object replace.

assets.alt: Object storage layout: bucket, key, index, replicas

blocks.subTitle: The S3 object model
blocks.markdown:
An object store is three concepts: bucket, key, object.

- **Bucket** — a named, flat namespace.
- **Key** — the object's full name like `users/42/avatar.png`; the slashes are *just characters*, there are no real folders.
- **Object** — the bytes plus metadata. You PUT under a key, GET by key.
- **Immutable** — you replace the whole object atomically; no append, no in-place edit.
- **Strongly consistent** since 2020 — a GET after a successful PUT always returns the latest bytes.

blocks.subTitle: B-tree engines
blocks.markdown:
A B+tree is a balanced tree of fixed-size sorted **pages** (4–16 KB). It updates data in place.

- A lookup walks root→leaf — only ~3–4 page reads for a billion keys, mostly served from cache.
- Writes find the leaf, modify it, write it back; a small change can rewrite a whole page (write amplification).
- A **write-ahead log (WAL)** records the change first, so a crash can be replayed ([relational-db-internals](relational-db-internals)).
- Win: data is always sorted and in one place → fast, predictable point reads and range scans.

blocks.subTitle: LSM-tree engines
blocks.markdown:
An LSM turns it inside out: never random-write, always append.

![LSM-tree write path: memtable to SSTable to compaction](assets/storage-systems/lsm-write-path.svg)

- A write lands in the in-RAM **memtable** and the **WAL** for durability.
- When the memtable fills, it flushes to an immutable, sorted **SSTable** on disk.
- A **delete** writes a **tombstone** marker — nothing is erased immediately.
- A read checks the memtable, then SSTables newest-to-oldest; a **Bloom filter** per SSTable cheaply says "key definitely not here."
- **Compaction** merges SSTables in the background, dropping dead data.

assets.alt: LSM-tree write path: memtable to SSTable to compaction

blocks.subTitle: The amplification triangle
blocks.markdown:
Three numbers describe any engine's cost, and they fight each other.

![B-tree vs LSM-tree trade-off](assets/storage-systems/btree-vs-lsm.svg)

- **Write amp** — physical bytes written ÷ logical. LSM compaction can rewrite a value 10–30×.
- **Read amp** — physical reads ÷ logical. An LSM read may probe many SSTables; a B-tree touches ~3–4 pages.
- **Space amp** — disk used ÷ live data. Stale copies inflate it until compaction runs.
- **RUM conjecture** — you optimize at most two of read, update, memory. Push one down, another pops up.

blocks.subTitle: Durability: replication vs erasure coding
blocks.markdown:
A single disk fails ~1–2% a year, so durability means redundant copies.

- **Replication** — keep N full copies on different machines. With 3 copies you survive 2 losses; simple and fast, but 3× storage.
- **Erasure coding** — split into *k* data + *m* parity shards; any *k* reconstruct the object. A 10+4 scheme survives 4 losses at only **1.4×** overhead.
- EC costs CPU to encode/decode and network on rebuild, so it suits large cold data; hot data stays replicated.
- **Eleven nines** (99.999999999%) = spread shards across AZs, scrub for bit rot, re-replicate on failure.

blocks.subTitle: B-tree vs LSM
blocks.markdown:
Same job — store sorted key-values — opposite corners of the triangle.

| Aspect | B-tree | LSM-tree |
|---|---|---|
| Writes | In place, random | Sequential append |
| Reads | Low amp | Higher amp |
| Background | None | Compaction |
| Best for | Read/mixed OLTP | Write-heavy ingest |

Logs, metrics, event streams, high-ingest KV → LSM. General transactional apps with reads and updates → B-tree.

blocks.subTitle: Row vs columnar
blocks.markdown:
The layout should match the query shape.

- **Row store** keeps each record's fields together: `[id,name,country,amount]…`. Perfect for "give me this whole record" (OLTP).
- **Columnar store** keeps each column together: all `id`s, then all `country`s. `SUM(amount) GROUP BY country` reads only two columns and skips the rest.
- Columns compress brutally — run-length and dictionary encoding give 5–10× and order-of-magnitude faster scans.
- Columnar is bad for OLTP: updating one record touches many separate column files.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems
blocks.markdown:
The same handful of ideas runs the systems you use daily.

- **Amazon S3** — flat keys + immutable objects to scale horizontally; erasure-coded across AZs for eleven nines.
- **Cassandra / RocksDB** — LSM engines; Cassandra defaults to size-tiered (low write amp), RocksDB to leveled (low read/space amp).
- **PostgreSQL / InnoDB** — B+trees plus a WAL for crash recovery; the classic OLTP profile.
- **Parquet + BigQuery/Snowflake** — columnar files with per-chunk min/max stats so engines skip whole blocks.

blocks.subTitle: The blob-store media pattern
blocks.markdown:
Media-heavy systems (video, photos, backups) all use the same layout: bytes in object storage, metadata in a database, served via a CDN.

- Upload streams the file to S3 under a key; the DB records key, owner, size, status ([nosql-distributed-data](nosql-distributed-data)).
- A transcoding pipeline reads from S3 and writes resized variants back as new objects.
- Playback URLs point at a CDN that caches popular objects near users ([caching](caching)).
- The database holds *pointers*, never the heavy bytes — staying small and fast while object storage absorbs petabytes.

The mistakes that bite in interviews and production:

- **"S3 has folders."** Keys are flat strings; `/` is convention, and there's no atomic directory rename.
- **"LSM is always faster."** Only for write ingest; point-read-heavy work often runs better on a B-tree.
- **"More replicas = more durable."** Replicas don't stop correlated failures — bit rot, a bad deploy, or an erroneous delete. Spread across failure domains and version.
- **"Compaction is free."** It fights live traffic for CPU and I/O; untuned, it spikes tail latency.
- **"Object storage is a database."** No joins, no cross-object transactions — keep queryable metadata elsewhere.
